user: Explain in three sentences how a refrigerator keeps food cold.
answer: A refrigerator works by circulating a refrigerant fluid that absorbs heat from the air inside the unit and releases it outside through coils at the back or bottom. This process relies on the refrigerant changing states between liquid and gas, which allows it to efficiently transfer thermal energy away from the food compartment. As a result, the interior temperature remains lower than the surrounding environment, keeping food cold and slowing down spoilage.

user: # What It Takes to Run a 125B LLM Fast on a 64 GB Mac, and How to Go Faster *How batch-invariant speculative checks, SSD-streamed experts and a certified lossy layer build on each other within a 45 GB memory line, and what each piece adds.* Kamen Levi Independent researcher --- ## 0. Draft status (delete before release) - **v3-draft, Sun 8 Nov 2026, 19:5x (Mon 9 Nov 00:4x: chat as shipped with PF-D; Strata's file; DFlash2's source; 09:5x: the number check's first pass applied, 22 items; gates end 16:00; 10:3x: lossy rows re-based on CERT / L / L + COH, the shipped L + COH passed its card gate; 11:5x: frozen for the 12:00 full draft, open items in Appendix A). Dates: `MONDAY.md`** (full draft Mon 12:00; number check and related-work check 12:00-16:00; finals 18:00; the release happens only on the project owner's word). Since v2: every open item of sections 4-8 is filled or turned into a stated limit (Appendix A), section 12 is re-opened, and the abstract's ratios are like for like. Sections 9-10 aligned with STYLE.md (Sun 20:3x); Appendix F is a summary; its full form is [KERNELS] 4.4 and 6.3-6.5. v1.1 is kept as `MAIN_v1.1_2026-11-06.md`. - **The set.** This paper is [MAIN]. The companions are [SMALL-RAM], [KERNELS], [EVAL], [DRAFTER] and [RELEASE]; their shared words and metrics are in `STYLE.md`. Kernels, the certification method, the 32 / 24 / 12 GB lines and the drafter are told in full there and summarised here. - **Marks.** [K] measured, [P] priced, [G] judgement; the mark travels with the number. `[[TBD-n]]` = not measured yet. - **Speeds** are the STYLE.md triple: whole decode, whole request, first token, plus the lifetime peak, pooled over the named prompt set. The engine's run reports quote a geometric mean over prompts ("geo"), 0-8 % higher; both are in Appendix E (`MoonShots/papers/main_table.txt`, re-derived from the raw run records by `papers/main_table.py`). - **Checked for this version:** every number in sections 6-7 was re-read from the file named beside it on Sun 8 Nov (16:5x-19:5x), and the headings were checked for WITHDRAWN / CORRECTED. Section 8's rows and section 12's identifiers were re-opened on Sun 8 Nov (`MoonShots/research/relwork`, passes 1 and 2a); pass 2 (the companions' references, issue figures, community posts) runs Mon 12:00-16:00. Competitor numbers are self-reported unless we reproduced them. ### Outline (v2) - Abstract. - 1 Introduction: the setting, contributions, what we do not claim, the companion papers. - 2 Definitions and how we measure: exact (to which reference), lossy with same scores (on which benchmarks), gate open; the speed triple; pooled aggregation; the four 12-prompt sets; marks and sources. - 3 Exactness (short; [KERNELS] has the kernels): the definition, the references REF2 -> NAX6-N, the audits (36 prompts; E5 96 / 96; chat and math 24 / 24; chat after the coherent-read fix 12 / 12), changing a reference. - 4 The 45 GB system: model, store and SSD; cache and loader; the check loop; the exact default and its levers (new: cache keep, wired limit, the exact-safe bundle, coherent reads, the 1-row check); prefill (layer-major, exact); the memory line and where it is exceeded (agent prompts, 45.1 GB). - 5 The lossy configuration and its certificate (short; [EVAL] has the method): its parts; CERT (same scores on HumanEval+, MBPP, math and IFEval, both orders); chat is lossy, not exact; the chat lever M1-B and its open gate. - 6 Results: the 45 GB tables (exact, lossy-certified, chat gate open), prefill, and where a request's time goes. - 7 Same machine, same prompts: Strata (decode, whole request, first token; equal memory; break-even; caveats). - 8 Published runs and related work (re-checked Sun 8 and Mon 9 Nov; every row self-reported unless we reproduced it). - 9 Methods that carry to other models (the SSD wake penalty and keepalive; 3-bit kept experts on drafted rows; relaxed acceptance restricted to code comments). - 10 Negative results and corrected headlines (the steady metric; 157.9 and 40.8 withdrawn; larger prefill chunks change logits; never-wait; split; CD16; trellis; ...). - 11 What we left on the table. - 12 References. Appendices: A open items, B figures, C how the results were produced and the code release (GPL-3, MLX 0.32.2 + pad to 64), D ledger keys, E every row (pooled and geo, per pass). --- ## Abstract We run a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 48 layers, 512 routed experts per layer, 10 per token) on one MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, 64 GB, 2 TB SSD), with the routed experts streamed from the internal SSD at about 3.2 bits per weight and the process's lifetime peak at most 45 GB (plus a 7.45 GB expert tier that macOS may reclaim). The pieces are mostly published; this paper is about how they depend on each other and what each adds. Speculative decoding pays one pass of the large model for up to 16 drafted tokens, but it is exact only if that pass computes the same bits as one-token decoding. Batch-invariant kernels on the GPU and its matrix units make it so, and we audit it on every run (96 of 96 code runs, 24 of 24 chat and 24 of 24 math runs token-identical to one-token greedy decoding). Exactness then turns every later optimisation into a test of token equality that takes minutes: the levers of the streamed engine, such as per-layer expert pools and expert reads hidden behind the GPU's work, were each adopted that way. On top of the exact engine, a lossy layer lets drafted rows of code answers skip cold experts and run 3-bit parts, and ships only if it scores the same as the exact reference on the model's benchmarks. The exact configuration decodes 101.4 tok/s on 12 HumanEval prompts, 70.4 on 12 MBPP, 77.9 on 12 math and 37.1 on 12 chat (IFEval) prompts, at a lifetime peak of 41.7-42.5 GB [K]. The lossy configuration we ship scores the same as the exact reference on the model card's IFBench, GPQA Diamond and LiveCodeBench v6 in both prompt orders, and decodes 164.0, 112.7, 78.9 and 45.2 tok/s on the same sets at 42.4-43.2 GB [K]. Our first token is slow, a median of 2.7-4.6 s on these short prompts: on the same machine and prompts the open engine Strata's takes 0.54-1.01 s, and Strata wins or ties every whole request of up to 256 tokens, although our lossy decode is 2.5-3.5x its decode on code [K]. None of the methods is specific to this model's layers; we tested one model on one machine. Section 12 describes each finding that, to our knowledge, has not been published before, with its evidence, what it gives and its limits, including one idea that did not pay off. We also report negative results, including three headline numbers we corrected or withdrew. --- ## 1. Introduction ### 1.1 The setting - **The model.** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (arXiv 2608.30320) is an open-weight mixture-of-experts model with a hybrid trunk: 36 linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet, "GDN") layers and 12 full-attention layers, four residual streams joined by low-rank hyper-connection (HC) mixers, one shared expert and 512 routed experts per layer with 10 routed per token, and a multi-token-prediction (MTP) head. It has about 125B parameters in total (section 4.1). - **The machine.** One MacBook Pro, M5 Pro, 64 GB of unified memory, internal SSD. All numbers are for one user, greedy decoding. - **The problem.** At MLX 4-bit the routed experts alone are 67.9 GB [K, BM:FINDINGS.md section 1], so they cannot all stay in memory. A token reads about 2.46 GB of dense weights and 1.33 GB of routed experts [K, same]. Decoding one token at a time pays a full pass over the dense trunk per token. - **Speculative decoding** pays that pass once per check: a small drafter proposes a block of tokens and one pass of the large model verifies up to 16 of them. - **Why exactness is not free.** A verify pass computes 16 positions in one batched call; one-token decoding computes each in a 1-row call. On stock kernels those are different programs with different rounding: in our first screen all 16 rows differed from one-token decoding at layer 0 (section 3). A greedy decoder then drifts at near-ties, and "speculative decoding is lossless" stops being true. ### 1.2 The idea: known pieces that need each other The pieces build on published work; section 8 credits each one and says which part is ours, and the prior art is in Appendix I. Section 12 describes the findings of this work that, to our knowledge, have not been published before. What this paper adds is the order in which they depend on each other, and that they still work, exactly, when combined. Section 7 gives each step's measured effect, and says where a step was never measured alone. 1. **Exact checks.** Speculative decoding verifies up to 16 drafted tokens in one pass, but greedy decoding is unchanged only if that pass computes the same bits as 16 one-token steps. Batch-invariant kernels make it so (section 3; [KERNELS]). 2. **Optimisation by token equality.** With an exact reference, a change to the engine is accepted when every token equals the reference on a handful of prompts, in minutes, with no quality argument (section 3.3). Every lever of the 45 GB engine was adopted that way (section 4.4). 3. **A store that fits.** The routed experts (120.8B parameters) live on the SSD as aligned records with a 3-bit part and a 4th-bit sidecar; each layer keeps a pool of them in memory, and a token's two top-ranked experts read both parts while the other eight read the 3-bit part (sections 4.1-4.2). The check loop is what makes streaming affordable: a check pays the SSD reads for the union of its rows' experts once, and every token it keeps shares them. 4. **Hiding the reads.** Expert ids stay on the GPU, and resident experts compute while missed ones load (section 4.4). The experts' outputs are still summed in a fixed order, so both changes keep every token equal and were accepted as in step 2. 5. **A certified lossy layer.** On drafted rows of code answers the engine skips cold lower-ranked experts and runs the 3-bit part of the rest, and a few reads are made at lower precision everywhere (section 5). The check loop says which rows are drafted; the layer ships only if it scores the same as the exact reference of step 1 on the model's benchmarks. 6. **Prefill from the same store.** A short prompt can build its experts from the copies already in memory and read only what is missing (PF-D, shipped for chat); a long prompt can run each layer over the whole prompt, so that each expert is read about once (built, not shipped; section 4.5). ### 1.3 What carries to other models None of the methods depends on this model's linear-attention or hyper-connection layers (section 8). The exact check needs batch-invariant kernels for the model's operations; the store, the loader and the lossy row rules need a mixture of experts with a drafter. The design is meant as an engine for such models in general, but we tested one model on one machine, and that is the limit of what this paper shows. ### 1.4 Contributions 1. **Exact speculative checks at 125B on Apple silicon (section 3; kernels in [KERNELS]).** A 16-row check that equals 16 one-token steps bit for bit, audited on every measured run, and a rule for changing the reference. 2. **An engine built by token equality (sections 4 and 7).** An SSD-streamed store, cache and loader within a 45 GB memory line, each lever accepted by token equality, and an account of what each piece adds on top of the others and which steps were never measured alone. 3. **A lossy configuration certified on the model's benchmarks (section 5; method in [EVAL]).** The same scores as the exact reference on HumanEval+, MBPP, math and IFEval, and, for the configuration we ship, on the model card's IFBench, GPQA Diamond and LiveCodeBench v6, in both prompt orders. 4. **Methods that carry to other MoE models (section 8), a short comparison with other engines (section 9), and negative results (section 10) and the path to more speed (section 11).** 5. **New findings (section 12).** Findings that, to our knowledge, have not been published before, each with its evidence, what it gives, what is measured and what is still a hypothesis, and how it could be improved. ### 1.5 What we do not claim - **Not the fastest engine for this model.** Our first token is 2.7-7.0x slower than Strata's on the same machine, and engines with lower-bit files or on larger Macs report a faster decode or prefill (self-reported; section 9). Our decode leads on code and math, slightly on chat in the lossy mode, and by a wide margin only in the lossy mode on code. - **Not new pieces.** Every lever in the measured configurations builds on published work, credited in section 8 and Appendix I; the findings that are, to our knowledge, new are in section 12. What we add is making them work together, exactly, at this size on this hardware, and measuring what each adds. To our knowledge no published engine for this model combines all of them; Strata and Sushi combine several (section 9). - **Not exact to the original 4-bit weights.** "Exact" always names a reference (section 2); ours runs ranks 0-1 of each token's experts at 4 bits and ranks 2-9 at 3 bits. ### 1.6 The companion papers [KERNELS] has the batch-invariant kernels and the MLX findings; [EVAL] the certification method and its pitfalls; [DRAFTER] the drafter work, including what failed; [RELEASE] the engine package (GPL-3). The 32, 24 and 12 GB lines are the subject of a forthcoming companion paper ([SMALL-RAM], by 11 November 2026); no number in this paper depends on it. This paper states each companion's results in one sentence where it needs them. ## 2. Definitions and how we measure - **Exact (to R).** The output tokens, and the logits row behind every kept token, are bit-identical to one-token greedy decoding under reference R, a fixed set of weights, kernels and call shapes. Changing a kernel changes rounding and makes a new reference, which is accepted once on task scores (section 3.4). Our 45 GB reference is NAX6-N. - **Lossy, same scores on <sets>.** A configuration that changes which computation a row runs, accepted only after its pre-registered same-scores gate against its exact reference on the named known benchmarks, in two prompt orders. Never "same quality". - **Lossy, gate open** (a gate is running or undecided) and **lossy, ungated** (no gate). Every configuration in this paper carries one of these labels. - **Speed** comes as a triple for a named prompt set: - whole decode = generated tokens / decode wall time (prefill excluded, every check included); - whole request = generated tokens / (first token time + decode wall time); - first token = request start to the first generated token, including prefill and setup (median and range); - plus the lifetime peak memory footprint of the process (ri_lifetime_max_phys_footprint, which counts the GPU's buffers), in GB of 10^9 bytes; the 45 GB line is 41.9 GiB [K, ES:evalsuite/decode.py, footprint_peak_gb]; - not counted in it: a 7.45 GB volatile expert tier (64 / 32 slots per base / sidecar pool), purgeable memory that macOS reclaims before it compresses or swaps; every run log behind Table 6.1 states it [K, e.g. BM:data/rel/rli_160.txt line 7]. - **Aggregation.** Pooled over prompts and passes (total tokens / total time). The engine's run reports quote a geometric mean over prompts ("geo"), 0-8 % higher on our sets; both are in Appendix E. - **Workloads.** 12 HumanEval and 12 MBPP prompts (the same ids in every run), 12 IFEval prompts as our chat set and 12 math (MATH-500) prompts; greedy, at most 256 new tokens, EOS stop. HumanEval flatters: 67.8 % of the generated tokens on our 12 HumanEval prompts copy the prompt's own signature and docstring [K, F:lossy350-thinking-hour], which drafting accepts cheaply. We never quote HumanEval without MBPP or chat beside it. - **The machine during runs.** Other jobs were stopped through a GPU lock ("quiet"); a run's report lists pauses for heat and drops any request that overlaps one. - **Marks.** [K] measured, [P] priced (arithmetic or a CPU replay on measured data), [G] judgement. Every number names its source (a run record, report or result file); Appendix C maps the keys to paths. - **The memory line.** "45 GB" means the run's lifetime peak is at most 45.0 GB. It is the engine's own footprint on a 64 GB machine, not a limit the operating system enforces. ## 3. Exactness (details in [KERNELS]) ### 3.1 References | reference | what it is | status | |---|---|---| | REF2 | batch-invariant kernel set: every matmul, HC read and attention call padded to 16 rows, routed experts on one 16-row tile kernel, a load-time self-test | adopted 28 Oct (T1210) | | REF2b | REF2 + attention key buckets past 512 keys, attention classes below 128 keys, the commit phase and slot call | adopted 31 Oct (T1219) | | REF2-T | REF2b on rank-tiered experts: ranks 0-1 at 4 bits, ranks 2-9 at 3 bits | 1 Nov (T1214, T307) | | NAX6-N | REF2-T with the routed experts on a matrix-unit kernel over records in the kernel's native layout | certified 5 Nov; the 45 GB exact reference (EV:RESULT_nax6_2026-11-05) | The first screen compared 16 one-token steps with one 16-row verify on identical caches, layer by layer: with the shipped kernels all 16 rows diverged at layer 0, because the framework picks a different matmul kernel by row count; attention, long context (past 512 keys) and short context (below 128 keys) broke next [K, LT:'R-40 REF2'; T1225; T1208; T1218]. The fixes and the kernels are [KERNELS]'s subject. ### 3.2 The audits Each audit decodes every prompt twice, with the speculative loop and one token at a time, and compares every kept row. | reference and arm | prompts | result | source | |---|---|---|---| | REF2b | 36 full-length (12 code, 12 math, 12 IFEval) | 16,305 / 16,305 kept rows bitwise; 15 / 15 prompts past 512 keys, 6 / 6 past 1,024 | EV:RESULT_r56b_2026-10-31 | | NAX6-N + out-of-order experts | same 36 | 15,690 / 15,690 kept rows bitwise; out-of-order path engaged on every tier call | EV:RESULT_nax6_2026-11-05, Part 2 | | the exact default (E, EB) on code | 12 HumanEval + 12 MBPP, 2 arms x 2 passes | 96 / 96 runs token-identical to one-token decoding | F:2026-11-07_1735 | | EB on chat and math | 12 IFEval + 12 math, 2 passes | 24 / 24 and 24 / 24 | F:2026-11-07_2330 | | E + coherent reads (+ the 1-row check) on chat | 12 IFEval | 12 / 12 in two runs (37.8 / 37.9 tok/s) and 12 / 12 (38.3); without coherent reads 3 / 12 | F:2026-11-08_0750 | | layer-major prefill | 3 agent prompts, 1.6K-7.9K tokens | decode tokens equal; logits hash equal on 8 / 8, 28 / 28, 22 / 22 checks | F:2026-11-08_0800 | - **The chat failure and its fix.** A one-call path for chat checks made exact chat nondeterministic (3 of 12 prompts equal). Coherent reads in the expert kernel restored 12 of 12 at no cost (F:2026-11-08_0750); [KERNELS] has the mechanism. - **The audit is part of every run.** Each exact row of section 6 carries its own token-identity count. It is how two bugs were caught that speed numbers alone hide: a fast path that never engaged (T18) and a kernel that was silently bypassed (F:flat2, caveat). ### 3.3 What exactness buys Once a reference exists, an optimisation is accepted by token equality on a handful of prompts, in minutes, with no quality argument. Every lever of section 4.4 was accepted this way. It has a price: the batch-invariant one-token path ran at x0.75 of stock kernels (11.65 vs 15.50 tok/s over 210 rows, row time with prefill included; information only) [K, EV:RESULT_ref2_2026-10-28; [KERNELS] R31]. ### 3.4 Changing the reference: certified once, on scores A new reference moves bits, so it is judged on tasks, once, by a rule fixed in advance ("decision 4"): on each of three sets (math, n 50; IFEval, n 100, strict prompt level; HumanEval+, n 60, pass@1) the paired score difference must be above -5 points and the exact McNemar p at least 0.05. | new reference vs old | math | IFEval | HumanEval+ | verdict | source | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | REF2 vs the previous reference | +8.0 | -3.0 | 0.0 | PASS | EV:RESULT_ref2_2026-10-28 | | REF2b vs the previous reference | +6.0 | -3.0 | 0.0 | PASS | T1219 | | REF2-T vs REF2b | 0.0 | +3.0 | +3.3 | PASS | T307 | | NAX6 vs REF2-T | 0.0 | -3.0 (p 0.375) | -3.3 (p 0.50) | PASS | EV:RESULT_nax6_2026-11-05 | These are same-score tests on 210 items, not proofs of equal quality: pooled over the NAX6 sets, NAX6 alone is right on 2 items and REF2-T alone on 7 (two-sided p 0.18). A further kernel bundle (REF2c-T) failed the rule on IFEval (-5.0) and was not adopted. The gaps chain: the certified lossy config of section 5 is -8.33 points on the HumanEval+ core set against REF2-T, two references back (forward order, p 0.0625), which no gate of its own measured [K, F:2026-11-08_0455; information]. ## 4. The 45 GB system ### 4.1 Model, store and hardware | part | parameters | notes | |---|---|---| | routed experts | 120.8 B | 48 layers x 512 experts, top-10; one expert = gate/up [1280 x 2560] + down [2560 x 640] | | linear attention (GDN) | 2.09 B | 36 of 48 layers | | full attention + indexer | 0.62 B | 12 layers, 24 query heads, 2 key/value heads, head dim 256 | | hyper-connections | 0.64 B | 4 residual streams, low-rank mixers | | embedding / output head / shared expert / router | 0.64 / 0.64 / 0.24 / 0.06 B | one shared expert per layer | | MTP head | 2.61 B | one layer with its own 512 experts | | n-gram tables | 51.2 B | layer 1 only; 16 rows read per token, from the SSD | Source: BM:FINDINGS.md section 1 (config and safetensors headers). **Active per token [P, arithmetic on this table]:** 10 of 512 routed experts in each of 48 layers (480 x 4.92 M = 2.36 B), attention 2.71 B, hyper-connections 0.64 B, the shared expert and router 0.30 B: 6.0 B, or 6.65 B with the output head. The 125.7 B total counts the rows above except the MTP head, the vision tower and the n-gram tables (16 rows of 160 values read per token); with them the checkpoint stores 180 B, the size some engines quote for this model (Kapitsa, Mference; Appendix H). Our engine runs this architecture through the model code of MTPLX by Youssof Altoukhi (Apache-2.0; github.com/youssofal/mtplx); the store, the kernels and the check loop are ours. - **Records.** Each expert is one contiguous, 16 KB-aligned record, read with one call that bypasses the page cache (F_NOCACHE): an MSB part (the 3 most significant bits of every weight with scales and biases) and an LSB sidecar (the 4th bit). The 4-bit weights are rebuilt bit-exactly from the two parts; the store is 68.5 GB on disk (48 layer files; 2.79 MB per expert record) [K, BM:models/bare/records3, the converter's output; not in the public snapshot]. For the matrix-unit kernel the records are stored in the kernel's own fragment order, with scales packed to 11 bits (bitwise; T527, T334). - **Rank tiers.** A token's two highest-scoring experts (ranks 0-1) run at 4 bits and read both parts; ranks 2-9 run from the MSB part alone. Expert bytes fall about 20 % (T307). - **The SSD.** Cold 2.77 MB reads reach 14.0 GB/s at queue depth 16 [K, BM:FINDINGS.md section 2]. In the engine the SSD time per check follows 10-16 ms plus 0.15-0.17 ms per missed expert [K, T288]. ### 4.2 Expert cache and loader - Each layer has a pool of expert slots in GPU memory; C 256 means 256 slots per layer on average, with per-layer sizes at equal memory (-17.2 % SSD bytes per kept token and +8.3 % tok/s, exact; T12, adapted from AdapMoE). Eviction is LRU. - All misses of a layer load in parallel, aligned, straight into slot memory (T7; M-29). Part of the pool is a volatile tier the operating system may reclaim (T1088). - **The wired limit.** MLX's wired Summarize the main findings of the document above in five bullet points.
answer:
Based on the document provided, here are the five main findings:

*   **Exact Speculative Decoding via Batch-Invariant Kernels:** The authors achieve bit-identical results between speculative decoding (verifying up to 16 tokens in one pass) and standard one-token decoding by using batch-invariant kernels. This ensures that the "lossless" claim of speculative decoding holds true, allowing every optimization to be validated simply by checking for token equality against a reference, rather than relying on statistical quality metrics.
*   **SSD-Streamed Expert Storage to Fit 125B Model in 64GB RAM:** To run the 125B-parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, the system streams routed experts from the internal SSD rather than keeping them all in memory. Experts are stored as aligned records with a 3-bit main part and a 4th-bit sidecar; the top two ranked experts per token run at 4-bit precision while the remaining eight run at 3-bit, allowing the process to stay within a 45 GB memory footprint (plus a reclaimable 7.45 GB volatile tier).
*   **Certified Lossy Configuration for Code Tasks:** A "lossy" configuration
